To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the energy distributions in a calorimeter can be parameterized by the negative binomial distribution and that the energy resolution can be improved by about a factor of two by applying the leakage correction method.

the energy resolution of the calorimeter depends on the energy, the type of particle and the sampling thickness, that the energy resolution is best for 1 GeV photons and 10 Gev electrons, and that the last-layer energy correction method improves the energy resolution for photons by a factor of two.
the energy resolution of electromagnetic showers can be improved by using a correction method based on the energy deposited in a thin layer close to the end of the calorimeter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the energy fluctuations of showers in segmented electromagnetic calorimeters, with the aim of improving the energy estimation.
the development of the methods of analysis of the data from the calorimeter of the COMPASS experiment.
the development of a high resolution CsI calorimeter, which will be installed in the KLOE detector at DAPHNE.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no simple and universal energy estimator.

the energy resolution of the calorimeter depends on the energy, on the type of particle, on the sampling, on the thickness of the layers, on the position of the shower maximum, and on the energy reconstruction method used.
a segmented CsI calorimeter with a sampling thickness of 1.08 X/sub 0/ and 1 cm thickness of the active medium, is a good calorimeter for electrons and photons in the range 1-10 GeV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the leakage corrections are very important and the energy estimation should be based on the total energy in the detector.
the energy estimation of electromagnetic calorimeters can be improved with a better understanding of shower development.
the energy resolution for electrons in CsI is 2-3 times better than that for photons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the energy fluctuations are very different for different energies and for different depths in the calorimeter.

the energy estimation of electromagnetic cascades is more complicated than the estimation of hadron showers, where the energy resolution is determined by the fluctuations in the number of particles in the last layer, and where the last-layer energy estimator is the most effective.

the energy estimation of electrons and photons in a segmented calorimeters is not trivial and that more work is needed to fully understand the energy resolution of electromagnetic showers in calorimeters.
